calc_items.title: WHO Plan B
calc_items.question: An 11-kg child with some dehydration is prescribed WHO Plan B ORS 75 mL/kg over 4 hours. Calculate the total ORS volume.

calc_items.title: WHO Plan C
calc_items.question: An 8-kg infant with severe dehydration, without shock, receives WHO Plan C: 100 mL/kg in total, first 30 mL/kg then 70 mL/kg. Calculate the volume of each phase.

calc_items.title: ORS for ongoing losses
calc_items.question: A 2-year-old has four additional watery stools and is prescribed 150 mL ORS after each. Calculate the replacement volume.
calc_items.working: 4 × 150 = 600 mL, in addition to the baseline/rehydration plan.

calc_items.title: Weight loss
calc_items.question: Pre-illness weight was 10.2 kg; current weight is 9.5 kg. Calculate the percentage weight loss from the baseline weight.

calc_items.title: Fractionated bilirubin
calc_items.question: Total bilirubin is 5 mg/dL and direct bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL. Calculate the direct fraction as a percentage (does a fraction below 20% exclude cholestasis?).
calc_items.working: 1.4/5 × 100 = 28%. No — an absolute direct bilirubin ≥1 mg/dL is concerning whatever the fraction.

calc_items.title: Maintenance fluid
calc_items.question: Using Holliday–Segar 100/50/20, calculate the 24-hour maintenance fluid estimate for a 24-kg child (before clinical adjustment).
calc_items.working: First 10 kg 1000 mL; next 10 kg 500 mL; final 4 kg 80 mL = 1580 mL/day.

calc_items.title: Stool osmotic gap
calc_items.question: Stool sodium is 40 mmol/L and potassium 30 mmol/L. Calculate the stool osmotic gap = 290 − 2(Na + K).
calc_items.working: 290 − 2(40 + 30) = 150 mOsm/kg; a high gap suggests an osmotic mechanism.

calc_items.title: Adenosine second dose (notebook repair)
calc_items.question: A stable 32-kg child with SVT: a named local protocol specifies second-dose adenosine 0.2 mg/kg rapid IV/IO push, maximum 12 mg. Calculate the dose.
calc_items.working: 0.2 × 32 = 6.4 mg, below the 12 mg maximum. Rapid IV/IO with flush and monitoring; check rhythm, contraindications and the current local protocol.

101.A: Type C is tubular, a duct without constriction; a cone narrowing at the pulmonary end is type A.
101.C: Type E is elongated with a constriction remote from the trachea edge, not a simple cone.
101.D: Type B is a short window-like duct with aortic-end narrowing, not a conical duct.

102.A: Classic GALT deficiency causes cataracts but with hepatic failure, coagulopathy and E. coli sepsis; their absence favours galactokinase deficiency.
102.B: ALDOB deficiency (hereditary fructose intolerance) presents after fructose or sucrose exposure with hypoglycaemia and liver dysfunction, not milk-related cataracts.
102.D: ATP7B deficiency is Wilson disease, presenting later in childhood with liver or neuropsychiatric disease, not neonatal cataracts.

103.A: 700 mL corresponds to 100 mL/kg/day, not the prescribed 130 mL/kg/day.
103.C: 1,300 mL comes from multiplying 130 by 10 kg instead of 7 kg.
103.D: 1,820 mL is double the correct product (130 x 7 x 2), a doubling error.

104.B: Cri-du-chat (5p deletion) causes a high-pitched cat-like cry and microcephaly but not the Greek-warrior helmet facies.
104.C: 22q11.2 deletion causes conotruncal heart disease, hypocalcaemia and thymic hypoplasia, not Greek-warrior helmet facies.
104.D: 7q11.23 deletion (Williams) causes elfin facies, supravalvar aortic stenosis and hypercalcaemia.

105.A: PES allows evaluation after 48 hours when hypoglycaemia persists; insisting on 72 hours misapplies the transitional window.
105.C: Hypoglycaemia persisting beyond 48 hours with low ketones is not physiological and needs evaluation.
105.D: Insulin may be undetectable in hyperinsulinism; suppressed ketones and FFA with a glucagon response indicate insulin action.

106.A: Jensen grade 1 is nasal cannula at or below 2 L/min; 3 L/min exceeds this.
106.B: Any qualifying respiratory support at 36 weeks PMA defines BPD; 3 L/min cannula is not no BPD.
106.C: Grade 3 requires invasive mechanical ventilation; nasal cannula is non-invasive support.

107.B: 24 weeks PMA is the age at birth; the first exam is deferred because treatable ROP does not develop that early.
107.C: 36 weeks PMA is far too late for a 24-week infant and risks missing treatment-requiring ROP.
107.D: 40 weeks PMA is term-equivalent age and would miss the window for timely treatment.

108.A: 5.2 is what 12.5 x 60 / 144 gives, i.e. using 60 instead of 90 mL/kg/day.
108.C: 10.4 is what 12.5 x 120 / 144 gives, i.e. using 120 instead of 90 mL/kg/day.
108.D: 12.5 simply restates the dextrose percentage instead of calculating the GIR.

109.A: Ketotic hypoglycaemia shows high ketones and a poor glucagon response, the opposite of these findings.
109.B: Fatty-acid oxidation defects show elevated FFA with low ketones; here FFA are suppressed.
109.D: Renal glucosuria does not cause hypoglycaemia with suppressed ketones and a brisk glucagon response.

110.B: Obstructed TAPVC causes progressive pulmonary oedema and death within hours to days; elective follow-up is lethal.
110.C: The duct is not the problem; obstructed pulmonary venous return needs surgical repair.
110.D: Oral iron is irrelevant to an obstructed TAPVC surgical emergency.
